warmup.q: A service handles requests on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Its database pool has 20 connections and a connection timeout of 250 ms, and in two years it has never timed out. You switch request handling to one virtual thread per request. At the next traffic peak, what happens first?
options: Nothing changes: the connection pool still caps the database at 20
Connection timeouts: every request in the peak now asks for one of 20 connections at once
The JVM runs out of memory creating virtual threads
Throughput drops, because virtual threads run code more slowly than platform threads
warmup.why: The fixed pool was a limit nobody wrote down: it never let more than 20 requests near the database. With a virtual thread each, every request in the peak reaches the connection pool together, and those that wait longer than 250 ms fail. The first option is half right: the pool still caps the database at 20 connections, but the waiting moved into the pool, where it turns into errors. A few thousand parked virtual threads fit easily in the heap, and virtual threads run code at the same speed.

sections.h: The old pool was a limit you never wrote down
sections.html:
Here is the quote service from this lesson's lab, as it runs in production today. It handles requests on a fixed pool of 10 platform threads. Nobody remembers exactly why 10, but the database pool has 10 connections.

Java
public final class QuoteService implements AutoCloseable {
    // 10 platform threads, because the database pool has 10 connections
    private final ExecutorService workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);

    public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) throws Exception {
        String tier = db.tier(request.customerId());    // 5 ms on a pooled connection
        BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(request.pair());      // 100 ms HTTP call
        return new Quote(request.customerId(), request.pair(), rate, fee(tier, request.amount()));
    }
}
Kotlin
class QuoteService(private val db: CustomerDb, private val fx: FxApi) : AutoCloseable {
    // 10 platform threads, because the database pool has 10 connections
    private val workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)

    fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote {
        val tier = db.tier(request.customerId)    // 5 ms on a pooled connection
        val rate = fx.rate(request.pair)          // 100 ms HTTP call
        return Quote(request.customerId, request.pair, rate, fee(tier, request.amount))
    }
}

The obvious migration is one line: replace newFixedThreadPool(10) with newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Do that in the lab and every test fails with connection pool: no connection after 30 ms.

The pool did two jobs. It ran the requests, and it made sure that no more than 10 of them could ever reach the database. The second job was never written down anywhere, but it's the reason the connection pool never had to wait. Virtual threads take over the first job and drop the second. In a burst of 300 requests, all 300 now ask for a connection at the same moment, and the pool's 30 ms borrow timeout was tuned for 10 callers.

So put the second job back, explicitly, around the one call that needs it:

Java
private final Semaphore dbPermits = new Semaphore(db.poolSize(), true);   // one permit per pooled connection

public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) throws Exception {
    String tier;
    dbPermits.acquire();
    try {
        tier = db.tier(request.customerId());           // only the database call waits its turn
    } finally {
        dbPermits.release();
    }
    BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(request.pair());          // FX calls now overlap freely
    return new Quote(request.customerId(), request.pair(), rate, fee(tier, request.amount()));
}
Kotlin
private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true)        // one permit per pooled connection

fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote {
    val tier = withDbPermit { db.tier(request.customerId) }  // only the database call waits its turn
    val rate = fx.rate(request.pair)                         // FX calls now overlap freely
    return Quote(request.customerId, request.pair, rate, fee(tier, request.amount))
}

Why not just raise the pool's timeout? You could, and requests would wait inside the pool instead. The semaphore is better for two reasons. Its queue is visible: queueLength is a gauge you can put on a dashboard. And the policy is yours: wait, or tryAcquire with a deadline that fits the request's budget and fails before any work is done. Meanwhile the FX calls, which never needed a limit, go from 10 in flight to about 200.

try.title: Migrate in two steps
steps: Read MigrationDemo. 300 requests arrive at once. Each borrows one of 10 connections for a 5 ms query (the pool gives up after 30 ms), then makes a 100 ms FX call.
Predict, for A (the old pool), B (a plain swap to virtual threads) and C (virtual threads plus a Semaphore(10)): total time, failed requests, and peak FX calls in flight.
Run it. Then change C's semaphore to new Semaphore(3, true) (in Kotlin, Semaphore(3, true)) and predict the new time before running again.

code.title: MigrationDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l06; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * 300 quote requests arrive at once. Each borrows a connection from a 10-connection pool for a * 5 ms query (the pool gives up after 30 ms of waiting), then makes a 100 ms FX call. * The same handler runs three ways: the old fixed pool, a plain swap to virtual threads, * and virtual threads with a Semaphore in front of the database. */ public class MigrationDemo { static final int REQUESTS = 300; static final int CONNECTIONS = 10; static final Semaphore pool = new Semaphore(CONNECTIONS); // the fake connection pool static final AtomicInteger fxInFlight = new AtomicInteger(); static final AtomicInteger fxPeak = new AtomicInteger(); static String query() throws InterruptedException { if (!pool.tryAcquire(30, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { throw new IllegalStateException("connection pool: no connection after 30 ms"); } try { Thread.sleep(5); // the query return "standard"; } finally { pool.release(); } } static String fxRate() throws InterruptedException { fxPeak.accumulateAndGet(fxInFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(100); // the FX call return "1.0842"; } finally { fxInFlight.decrementAndGet(); } } interface Handler { String handle() throws Exception; } static void run(String label, ExecutorService executor, Handler handler) throws InterruptedException { fxPeak.set(0); int ok = 0, failed = 0; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (executor) { List<Future<String>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < REQUESTS; i++) futures.add(executor.submit(handler::handle)); for (Future<String> f : futures) { try { f.get(); ok++; } catch (ExecutionException e) { failed++; } } } System.out.printf("%-34s %,6d ms ok %3d failed %3d FX calls in flight at peak %3d%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ok, failed, fxPeak.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { // A: today: 10 platform threads, sized to the pool run("A: fixed pool of 10", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10), () -> query() + fxRate()); // B: the one-line migration: nothing limits the database any more run("B: virtual threads", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), () -> query() + fxRate()); // C: virtual threads, and the limit made explicit around the database call only Semaphore dbPermits = new Semaphore(CONNECTIONS, true); run("C: virtual threads + Semaphore(10)", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), () -> { String tier; dbPermits.acquire(); try { tier = query(); } finally { dbPermits.release(); } return tier + fxRate(); }); } }

Each borrows a connection from a 10-connection pool for a * 5 ms query (the pool gives up after 30 ms of waiting), then makes a 100 ms FX call. * The same handler runs three ways: the old fixed pool, a plain swap to virtual threads, * and virtual threads with a Semaphore in front of the database. */ private const val REQUESTS = 300 private const val CONNECTIONS = 10 private val pool = Semaphore(CONNECTIONS) // the fake connection pool private val fxInFlight = AtomicInteger() private val fxPeak = AtomicInteger() private fun query(): String { check(pool.tryAcquire(30, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { "connection pool: no connection after 30 ms" } try { Thread.sleep(5) // the query return "standard" } finally { pool.release() } } private fun fxRate(): String { fxPeak.accumulateAndGet(fxInFlight.incrementAndGet()) { a, b -> maxOf(a, b) } try { Thread.sleep(100) // the FX call return "1.0842" } finally { fxInFlight.decrementAndGet() } } private fun run(label: String, executor: ExecutorService, handler: () -> String) { fxPeak.set(0) var ok = 0 var failed = 0 val t0 = System.nanoTime() executor.use { val futures = List(REQUESTS) { executor.submit(Callable { handler() }) } for (f in futures) { try { f.get() ok++ } catch (e: ExecutionException) { failed++ } } } println("%-34s %,6d ms ok %3d failed %3d FX calls in flight at peak %3d" .format(label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ok, failed, fxPeak.get())) } fun main() { // A: today: 10 platform threads, sized to the pool run("A: fixed pool of 10", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)) { query() + fxRate() } // B: the one-line migration: nothing limits the database any more run("B: virtual threads", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { query() + fxRate() } // C: virtual threads, and the limit made explicit around the database call only val dbPermits = Semaphore(CONNECTIONS, true) run("C: virtual threads + Semaphore(10)", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { dbPermits.acquire() val tier = try { query() } finally { dbPermits.release() } tier + fxRate() } }

try.expect: A takes about 3,200 ms with no failures, and FX peaks at exactly 10. B is fast but most requests fail (one run here: 71 ok, 229 failed), because they all waited inside the pool. C takes about 260 ms with no failures, and FX peaks near 200. With 3 permits (the label still says 10), C takes about 600 ms: 300 queries × 5 ms / 3 permits is 500 ms, plus one 100 ms FX call, and FX peaks lower, near 60. The database part of the request decides the time, and the semaphore is where you choose it.

sections.html:
Every migration I have seen needed the same handful of changes. Go through them in this order.

  1. Run JDK 25 first. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier, and JDBC drivers, HTTP clients and logging appenders do exactly that. On JDK 25, only class initializers and native frames still pin. Lesson 4 of this track has the details.
  2. Replace the pools that run blocking work with one virtual thread per task, through newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() or your framework's switch. Delete the old pool-size setting so nobody tunes it later.
  3. For each downstream the old pool protected, write the limit down. That means one shared Semaphore per downstream, sized from what that downstream allows, held only around its calls. Also look for downstreams with no limit at all, because now nothing slows the traffic in front of them.
  4. Leave the connection pool small. A database runs well with a few connections per CPU core of the database server, and more connections make it slower. Every pod multiplies the number: 30 pods with 20 connections each are 600 sessions on one Oracle instance.
  5. Hunt ThreadLocals. Caches become one object per request (lesson 4 of this track), and request context belongs in arguments or scoped values (lesson 5).
  6. Keep CPU-heavy steps on a bounded pool of platform threads. Signing a settlement file on a virtual thread holds a carrier for the whole time.
  7. Give every wait a deadline. With a pool, a slow downstream filled the queue and callers got rejected. With virtual threads, nothing pushes back, and parked requests pile up in the heap. Use tryAcquire with a timeout and HTTP client timeouts, and return a fast 503 when you're over budget.

Item 3 is the one teams skip, because the code still works in tests. It only fails at the first real traffic peak.

In a real service, expect more pools than you thought: many of them sit inside libraries and framework config, not in your own code.

sections.h: Quarkus and Spring Boot: the switch is one line
sections.html:
Most services don't create their request threads themselves. The framework does, so the switch is in the framework.

Quarkus has no global switch. You opt in per endpoint, or per class, with @RunOnVirtualThread, and Quarkus then runs each call on a new virtual thread:

Java
@Path("/quotes")
public class QuoteResource {
    @Inject QuoteService quotes;

    @POST
    @RunOnVirtualThread                       // each call runs on a new virtual thread
    public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) {
        return quotes.quote(request);         // plain blocking code: JDBC, REST client, Kafka producer
    }
}
Kotlin
@Path("/quotes")
class QuoteResource(private val quotes: QuoteService) {

    @POST
    @RunOnVirtualThread                       // each call runs on a new virtual thread
    fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote =
        quotes.quote(request)                 // plain blocking code: JDBC, REST client, Kafka producer
}

The annotation is io.smallrye.common.annotation.RunOnVirtualThread. The same annotation works on Reactive Messaging @Incoming methods, which is how a Kafka consumer handles records on virtual threads. Opting in one endpoint at a time is a good fit for a migration: you move the busiest blocking endpoint first and compare.

Spring Boot 3.2 and later has one property for the whole application:

spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true

With it, the embedded web server handles requests on virtual threads, and Spring's own task executors use them too.

Neither framework adds the limits from the checklist. That's still your code. They also change what an old setting means. quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads sizes the worker pool, which @RunOnVirtualThread endpoints don't use, so it no longer caps them. If you relied on it as your database limit, that limit is gone, exactly like the pool in the lab.

The Quarkus guide lists the traps it sees most, and you know all of them by now: libraries that pin on JDK 21, CPU-heavy endpoints that monopolize a carrier, and libraries that pool objects in ThreadLocals.

sections.h: Measure it, and let Little's law find the bottleneck
sections.html:
Measure before you switch, then again after, with the same load test. You need a baseline of throughput, p50 and p99 latency, error rate, CPU, heap and GC time. Without it, "it feels faster" is all you'll have.

After the switch, one number stops meaning anything: the thread count. Fifty thousand virtual threads is normal and tells you nothing. Watch where requests wait instead:

  • requests in flight in the service
  • the queue length on each downstream semaphore
  • the connection pool's pending and active counts (HikariCP's Micrometer metrics are hikaricp.connections.pending and hikaricp.connections.active)
  • jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events from a JFR recording, as in lesson 4 of this track

Little's law ties these together: requests in flight = throughput × time in the system. Use it both ways. To predict, multiply: 400 requests per second that spend 120 ms in the service means about 48 in flight. To find a bottleneck, divide a limit by the time each request holds it. Ten database permits held for 20 ms each serve at most 10 / 0.02 s = 500 requests per second. Below that rate the semaphore's queue stays near zero. Above it, the queue grows every second, latency grows with it, and throughput stays flat at about 500. A rising queue gauge with flat throughput is what a saturated downstream looks like, and it is the alert to set up.

Roll out like any risky change. Switch one pod (or one endpoint in Quarkus), send it real traffic, and compare its numbers with the pods still on the old pool. Look at p99 latency and error rate first. Then check that heap and GC didn't jump, because parked virtual threads keep their stacks on the heap.

try.title: Watch a downstream saturate
steps: Read MeasureDemo. Requests arrive at a steady rate. Each holds one of 10 database permits for 20 ms, then makes a 100 ms FX call. A sampler prints two gauges every 250 ms.
Use Little's law to predict the requests in flight at 400 per second. Run it.
Work out the database's capacity from the permits and the query time. Then run it at 600 per second with -Pargs='600 2', and predict what the two gauges do first.

code.title: MeasureDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l06; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; import java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport; /** * Requests arrive at a steady rate, one virtual thread each. A request waits for one of 10 * database permits, runs a 20 ms query, then makes a 100 ms FX call. A sampler prints two * gauges you would put on a dashboard, and the summary checks Little's law: * requests in flight = throughput x time in the system. * * <p>Args: requests per second (default 400), seconds (default 2). */ public class MeasureDemo { static final Semaphore dbPermits = new Semaphore(10, true); static final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(); static final LongAdder done = new LongAdder(); static final LongAdder nanosInSystem = new LongAdder(); static volatile boolean stop; static void handle() { long start = System.nanoTime(); inFlight.incrementAndGet(); try { dbPermits.acquire(); try { Thread.sleep(20); // the database query } finally { dbPermits.release(); } Thread.sleep(100); // the FX call } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { inFlight.decrementAndGet(); nanosInSystem.add(System.nanoTime() - start); done.increment(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int rate = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 400; int seconds = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 2; long gapNanos = 1_000_000_000L / rate; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); // sample every 10 ms for the average; print every 250 ms long[] sums = new long[2]; // total in flight, number of samples Thread sampler = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().start(() -> { while (!stop) { LockSupport.parkNanos(10_000_000); sums[0] += inFlight.get(); sums[1]++; if (sums[1] % 25 == 0) { System.out.printf("t=%,5d ms in flight %4d waiting for a db permit %4d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, inFlight.get(), dbPermits.getQueueLength()); } } }); try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < rate * seconds; i++) { long due = t0 + i * gapNanos, wait; while ((wait = due - System.nanoTime()) > 0) LockSupport.parkNanos(wait); // steady arrivals perRequest.execute(MeasureDemo::handle); } } // waits for the last requests double elapsed = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9; stop = true; sampler.join(); double throughput = done.sum() / elapsed; // requests per second double timeInSystem = nanosInSystem.sum() / 1e9 / done.sum(); System.out.printf("throughput %.0f/s, mean time in system %.0f ms%n", throughput, timeInSystem * 1000); System.out.printf("Little's law: throughput x time = %.1f; measured average in flight = %.1f%n", throughput * timeInSystem, (double) sums[0] / sums[1]); } }

alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l06 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport /** * Requests arrive at a steady rate, one virtual thread each. A request waits for one of 10 * database permits, runs a 20 ms query, then makes a 100 ms FX call. A sampler prints two * gauges you would put on a dashboard, and the summary checks Little's law: * requests in flight = throughput x time in the system. * * Args: requests per second (default 400), seconds (default 2). */ private val dbPermits = Semaphore(10, true) private val inFlight = AtomicInteger() private val done = LongAdder() private val nanosInSystem = LongAdder() @Volatile private var stop = false private fun handle() { val start = System.nanoTime() inFlight.incrementAndGet() try { dbPermits.acquire() try { Thread.sleep(20) // the database query } finally { dbPermits.release() } Thread.sleep(100) // the FX call } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { inFlight.decrementAndGet() nanosInSystem.add(System.nanoTime() - start) done.increment() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val rate = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 400 val seconds = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 2 val gapNanos = 1_000_000_000L / rate val t0 = System.nanoTime() // sample every 10 ms for the average; print every 250 ms var totalInFlight = 0L var samples = 0L val sampler = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().start { while (!stop) { LockSupport.parkNanos(10_000_000) totalInFlight += inFlight.get() samples++ if (samples % 25 == 0L) { println("t=%,5d ms in flight %4d waiting for a db permit %4d" .format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, inFlight.get(), dbPermits.queueLength)) } } } Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest -> for (i in 0 until rate * seconds) { val due = t0 + i * gapNanos while (true) { // steady arrivals val wait = due - System.nanoTime() if (wait <= 0) break LockSupport.parkNanos(wait) } perRequest.execute { handle() } } } // waits for the last requests val elapsed = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9 stop = true sampler.join() val throughput = done.sum() / elapsed // requests per second val timeInSystem = nanosInSystem.sum() / 1e9 / done.sum() println("throughput %.0f/s, mean time in system %.0f ms".format(throughput, timeInSystem * 1000)) println("Little's law: throughput x time = %.1f; measured average in flight = %.1f" .format(throughput * timeInSystem, totalInFlight.toDouble() / samples)) }

try.expect: At 400 per second, requests in flight sit near 48 (400 × 0.12 s) and nobody waits for a permit. The summary's two Little's law numbers agree (45.7 and 45.7 in one run; they are a little below 48 because the averages include the start and the drain). The database's capacity is 10 / 0.02 s = 500 per second, so at 600 per second the permit queue grows on every line (44, 80, 113 and on to more than 200 in one run), time in the system climbs to around 400 ms, and throughput stays near 460 to 500. The thread count would have told you nothing; the queue gauge told you which downstream is full.

analogy: The old pool is a restaurant with 10 waiters and a kitchen with 10 burners. Nobody planned it, but with 10 waiters there are never more than 10 orders at the kitchen at once. Moving to virtual threads is like giving every table its own waiter the moment it's seated. Drinks and bread arrive at once, which is the FX call overlapping. But at a peak, 300 waiters crowd the kitchen door. The semaphore is a ticket machine at that door with 10 tickets: waiters queue in an orderly line you can count, and the kitchen works at its pace. The analogy breaks on cost. Real waiters are paid, so nobody would hire 300 by accident. Virtual threads cost almost nothing, so the crowd at the door can grow very large before anyone notices.
world: In a Quarkus service the datasource is an Agroal pool sized by quarkus.datasource.jdbc.max-size, and with @RunOnVirtualThread the worker pool no longer stands in front of it. Before you annotate the busiest endpoint, find out what used to cap it, and write that cap down as a semaphore. Do the same for each REST client: a card issuer that allows 150 calls in flight for your merchant, shared across 4 pods, means Semaphore(37) per pod. Size the Oracle side from the database, not from the thread count, and multiply by the number of pods. For a Kafka consumer moved to virtual threads, check how many records your framework now processes at once, and whether records with the same key still need to be handled in order. In a Temporal worker, the maximum number of concurrent activity executions is already an explicit limit. Size it from the downstreams the activities call, not from CPU.
mistake: The most common mistake is growing the connection pool to match the new concurrency: "we have 2,000 virtual threads now, so set the pool to 2,000". The database can only run a limited number of queries at once, roughly a few per CPU core of the database server. Past that point, more connections add context switching and lock contention inside the database, and every pod multiplies the session count. The result is a slower database and, at a peak, a database that refuses new sessions for every service that shares it. Keep the pool small and put an explicit semaphore in front of it. Then let requests queue in your service, where you can see the queue and shed load with a deadline.

compare.title: The migrated QuoteService in Java and Kotlin

java.title: QuoteService.java
java.html: public final class QuoteService implements AutoCloseable { private final CustomerDb db; private final FxApi fx; // 1. one new virtual thread per request: no size to pick private final ExecutorService requests = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // 2. the limit the old pool gave you by accident, now explicit private final Semaphore dbPermits; public QuoteService(CustomerDb db, FxApi fx) { this.db = db; this.fx = fx; this.dbPermits = new Semaphore(db.poolSize(), true); // one permit per pooled connection } public Quote quote(QuoteRequest r) throws Exception { String tier; dbPermits.acquire(); // outside the try try { tier = db.tier(r.customerId()); // only the database call holds a permit } finally { dbPermits.release(); } BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(r.pair()); // FX calls overlap freely return new Quote(r.customerId(), r.pair(), rate, fee(tier, r.amount())); } // 3. a gauge for the dashboard public int dbWaiting() { return dbPermits.getQueueLength(); } @Override public void close() { requests.close(); // 4. waits for requests in flight } }

kotlin.title: QuoteService.kt (the lab's solution)
kotlin.html: class QuoteService(private val db: CustomerDb, private val fx: FxApi) : AutoCloseable { // 1. one new virtual thread per request: no size to pick private val requests = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // 2. the limit the old pool gave you by accident, now explicit private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true) // one permit per pooled connection fun quote(r: QuoteRequest): Quote { val tier = withDbPermit { db.tier(r.customerId) } // only the database call holds a permit val rate = fx.rate(r.pair) // FX calls overlap freely return Quote(r.customerId, r.pair, rate, fee(tier, r.amount)) } // 3. a gauge for the dashboard fun dbWaiting(): Int = dbPermits.queueLength override fun close() = requests.close() // 4. waits for requests in flight private inline fun <T> withDbPermit(block: () -> T): T { dbPermits.acquire() // outside the try try { return block() } finally { dbPermits.release() } } }

compare.note: The migration is the same in both: the executor changes, and the limit becomes a semaphore around one call. Kotlin's version reads better because a small inline function with a lambda wraps acquire, try and release, and inlining means the lambda costs nothing at run time. Java has no equivalent without a functional interface, so the try/finally sits in the method. Two Kotlin traps: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore has a withPermit too, but it suspends a coroutine and is not the java.util.concurrent.Semaphore your threads need. And Kotlin doesn't check exceptions, so nothing reminds you that acquire() can throw InterruptedException. It still can, and it must still sit outside the try.

worked.title: Size every limit with Little's law before the switch

steps.say: A card authorization service runs on 4 pods, and each pod gets 200 requests per second at peak. A request holds a database connection for 15 ms, calls the fraud API for 200 ms, and calls the card issuer for 120 ms. The issuer allows 150 calls in flight for your merchant, across all pods. Today each pod has a fixed pool of 50 threads and 10 connections. First question: is the thread pool the bottleneck today?
steps.code:
time in the system   W = 15 + 200 + 120 ms = 335 ms
threads needed       L = 200/s x 0.335 s  = 67
the pool has 50, so at peak requests queue for a thread
pool capacity            50 / 0.335 s     = about 149 requests/s

steps.say: Yes. The pool tops out near 149 requests per second, below the 200 that arrive, so requests queue at peak. Virtual threads remove that limit. Now check each downstream with the same formula, because nothing caps them any more.
steps.code:
database connections busy   200/s x 0.015 s = 3      pool of 10: fine
issuer calls in flight      200/s x 0.120 s = 24     limit 150 / 4 pods = 37 per pod
fraud calls in flight       200/s x 0.200 s = 40     no published limit: ask the fraud team
virtual threads             67 at a time, a small amount of heap

steps.say: Write the limits in code: one shared semaphore per downstream, sized per pod, held only around that downstream's calls.
steps.code: final class Downstreams { // 1. issuer: 150 calls in flight for the merchant, shared by 4 pods final Semaphore issuer = new Semaphore(150 / 4, true); // 2. database: one permit per pooled connection final Semaphore db = new Semaphore(10, true); // 3. fraud: no limit yet; add one when the fraud team gives you a number }

alt.html: class Downstreams { // 1. issuer: 150 calls in flight for the merchant, shared by 4 pods val issuer = Semaphore(150 / 4, true) // 2. database: one permit per pooled connection val db = Semaphore(10, true) // 3. fraud: no limit yet; add one when the fraud team gives you a number }

steps.say: Predict where each limit starts to bite, by dividing permits by the time each request holds one. The issuer semaphore starts to queue at 37 / 0.12 s, about 308 requests per second per pod, and the database at 10 / 0.015 s, about 666. If one pod dies, the other 3 get about 267 per second each, still under 308. So the first alert to set is the issuer semaphore's queue length, and the capacity of the service is now about 300 requests per second per pod instead of 149.

lab.title: Migrate the quote service
steps: This lab is in Kotlin. Run the tests once. Four of five fail. The burst test passes, because the old pool of 10 keeps the database safe by accident.

TODO 1: replace Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Run the tests again. Now all five fail with connection pool: no connection after 30 ms. That's the limit you just removed.

TODO 2: add private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true) and hold a permit around the db.tier(...) call and nothing else: acquire() before a try, release() in its finally. A small private inline fun <T> withDbPermit(block: () -> T): T keeps quote readable.
TODO 3 and 4: dbWaiting() returns dbPermits.queueLength, and close() calls close() on the new executor.
Run the tests until all five pass. Then read the pool-size test: it builds a pool of 3 connections. Explain why Semaphore(10) would fail it.
hints: Keep the FX call outside the permit. If the permit covers the whole request, you have rebuilt the old 10-thread limit, and the FX test fails.
acquire() goes before the try. If it sat inside, a thread interrupted while waiting would release() a permit it never got, and the limit would quietly grow.
Import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, not kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore. The coroutine one suspends coroutines and doesn't work from a plain thread.
Semaphore.queueLength is an estimate while threads come and go, but it is exact when nothing changes, which is what the gauge test waits for.

drill.title: Write the migrated client from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write a LedgerClient that many virtual threads call at once through post(entry), and that never lets more than connections of them inside ledgerDb.insert(entry) at the same time. Callers that can't get in within 200 ms should fail fast with an exception. Then name the one metric you would export from it.

answer.html: final class LedgerClient { private final LedgerDb ledgerDb; private final Semaphore permits; // one per pooled connection, shared by all callers LedgerClient(LedgerDb ledgerDb, int connections) { this.ledgerDb = ledgerDb; this.permits = new Semaphore(connections, true); } void post(Entry entry) throws InterruptedException { if (!permits.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // a deadline, not an endless wait throw new LedgerBusyException("no ledger connection within 200 ms"); } try { ledgerDb.insert(entry); // only this call holds a permit } finally { permits.release(); } } int waiting() { // the metric: callers queued right now return permits.getQueueLength(); } }

alt.html: class LedgerClient(private val ledgerDb: LedgerDb, connections: Int) { private val permits = Semaphore(connections, true) // one per pooled connection, shared by all callers fun post(entry: Entry) { if (!permits.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // a deadline, not an endless wait throw LedgerBusyException("no ledger connection within 200 ms") } try { ledgerDb.insert(entry) // only this call holds a permit } finally { permits.release() } } fun waiting(): Int = permits.queueLength // the metric: callers queued right now }

recap: A fixed thread pool limits every downstream its threads touch. Moving to virtual threads removes that limit together with the pool.
Write each limit down: one shared Semaphore per downstream, sized from that downstream, held only around its calls.
Don't grow connection pools to match thread counts. The database decides how many connections help, and every pod multiplies them.
Checklist: JDK 25 first, one virtual thread per task, explicit limits, ThreadLocal caches and context, CPU work on a bounded pool, a deadline on every wait.
Quarkus opts in per endpoint with @RunOnVirtualThread; Spring Boot 3.2+ switches with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. Neither adds your limits.
Measure before and after. In-flight = throughput × time (Little's law), and a growing queue gauge with flat throughput marks the saturated downstream.

explain.prompt: Your manager asks why the team can't just flip the virtual threads switch in production tomorrow. Explain what the switch changes, what can break, and how you would roll it out and measure it.
explain.answer: The switch gives every request its own virtual thread, so blocking calls stop tying up a limited pool and many more requests can be in flight. That is the point, and it is also the risk: the old pool also limited how many requests reached the database and the other downstreams, without anyone writing that down. After the switch, a peak sends all of them at once, and the connection pool starts timing out or a partner API starts rejecting us. So before the switch I'd run JDK 25 to avoid synchronized pinning, add a shared semaphore per downstream sized from its real limit, keep the connection pool small, replace ThreadLocal caches, and keep CPU-heavy work on a bounded pool. For the rollout I'd take a baseline under a load test, switch one pod or one endpoint, and compare p99, error rate, heap and GC with the others. I'd also watch the semaphore queues and the pool's pending count, and use Little's law to predict at what rate each one saturates.

deeper.html:
Admission control at the door. The lab's semaphore waits without a deadline, deep inside the request. In a payment API it's often better to decide at the start: try to take every permit the request will need, or a single "requests in progress" permit sized from Little's law, with a short tryAcquire deadline, and answer 503 at once if you can't. Then you never call the fraud API for a request that would later time out at the database.

Pool timeouts versus semaphore waits. A pool's borrow timeout and a semaphore's deadline look alike, but they sit at different places. The pool timeout fires after the request has done part of its work and maybe holds other resources. A deadline at the semaphore, at the start of the call, fails before any of that. Keep the pool's timeout too, as a safety net for bugs in your own limits.

Fairness and the tail. A fair semaphore serves waiters in arrival order. That costs a little throughput and keeps p99 close to p50 during a burst. A non-fair one lets a newcomer grab a permit that was just released, which helps the average and hurts the unlucky waiters. For payment latency the tail matters more.

Thread dumps after the move. jstack shows carriers, not the thousands of parked virtual threads. jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json writes all of them, grouped by the executor or scope that owns them. Before an incident, practise finding the stack of one stuck request in such a dump.

When not to migrate. A service that is CPU-bound, or that already runs fully reactive code on a few event-loop threads, gains little. The win is largest for services that block on I/O and are limited by their thread pool today. Little's law tells you which kind yours is: compare the threads you need (rate × time) with the threads you have.
